title: 12. Cloud, Containers & Deployment: Canary Deployment
summary: Canary deployment is a release strategy that progressively shifts a small and growing fraction of production traffic — typically 1% → 5% → 25% → 100% — to a new version, evaluating health metrics at each stage and…
objectives: What is canary deployment, and how does it differ from blue-green and rolling deployment?
How does automated canary analysis work, and what statistical tests does it use?
What traffic-shifting mechanisms can a canary use, and what are their trade-offs?
How do you choose the canary percentages and soak times for a service?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Canary deployment is a release strategy that progressively shifts a small and growing fraction of production traffic — typically 1% → 5% → 25% → 100% — to a new version, evaluating health metrics at each stage and automatically rolling back if the new version regresses, so that bugs are caught by a few users before they reach everyone.
Every change to a production system carries risk — a bug, a performance regression, an unexpected interaction with real data — and the cost of that risk scales with how many users see the new version before it is verified. The most aggressive strategy is the big-bang release: deploy the new version to all servers, send all traffic to it, and hope nothing breaks. When it breaks, every user is affected and rollback is slow. The most cautious strategy is blue-green, which keeps the old version warm and switches traffic atomically — but the cutover still exposes all users to the new version at the same moment, so a subtle regression that only manifests under real load (a slow query plan, a memory leak, a third-party API change) is felt by everyone before it is noticed. Canary deployment closes this gap by releasing the new version to a tiny fraction of users first, watching metrics, and only expanding exposure if the new version is provably healthy. The name comes from the historical practice of carrying a caged canary into a coal mine: if the canary died, the miners evacuated before the toxic gas affected them. In software, the canary is the small group of users on the new version; if their metrics degrade, traffic rolls back before the rest of the user base is exposed.

The first concept is traffic shifting. A canary needs a router capable of sending a configurable percentage of traffic to the new version — a load balancer with weighted target groups (AWS ALB weighted forwarding), a service mesh with traffic splitting (Istio VirtualService, Linkerd traffic-split), a feature flag platform (LaunchDarkly, Unleash), or a DNS-based weighted policy (Route 53). The router splits traffic between the "stable" version (the current production) and the "canary" version (the new release) according to a percentage that the deployment orchestrator controls. Traffic is split by request, not by user, unless the router supports sticky routing — for canary it is often important that a user who sees the canary continues to see it, so that a session-based regression is visible. The mechanics differ across platforms: AWS ALB weighted target groups assign each request to a target group by weight; Istio splits traffic at the sidecar level, per pod; feature flags evaluate a user ID hash and route consistently. The choice of router determines the granularity of the canary (per-request vs per-user vs per-region) and the speed of shifting (seconds for ALB/Istio, minutes for DNS).

The second concept is the staged progression. A canary is not a single shift to 5% and then to 100% — it is a series of stages, each gated by metric analysis. A typical progression is 1% → 5% → 25% → 100%, with a "soak" period at each stage (5–30 minutes) during which the orchestrator collects metrics and compares them to the stable version's. The early stages (1%, 5%) catch the worst regressions — crashes, error-rate spikes, complete breakage. The middle stages (25%) catch load-dependent regressions that only appear under meaningful traffic — connection pool exhaustion, slow query plans, cache stampedes. The final stage (100%) is the cutover, after which the stable version is drained and the canary becomes the new stable. The exact percentages and soak times depend on the service's traffic volume and risk tolerance: a service with 1 million requests per second can gather statistically meaningful metrics at 1% canary in minutes, while a service with 100 requests per second may need 10% canary and 30 minutes to gather enough samples. Google's progressive deployment framework standardizes this as "0.1% → 1% → 5% → 50% → 100%" with automated metric gates between each stage; Netflix's Spinnaker uses "1% → 25% → 100%" with Kayenta-based canary analysis at each step.

The third concept is automated canary analysis. The bottleneck in any canary is the decision: at each stage, is the canary healthy enough to proceed, or should it roll back? A human staring at dashboards is slow (10–30 minutes per stage) and error-prone (subtle regressions are easy to miss in a wall of charts). Automated canary analysis, pioneered by Netflix's Kayenta and now standard in Argo Rollouts, Flagger, and Spinnaker, compares the canary's metrics to the stable version's using statistical tests and produces a score. Hard thresholds catch gross regressions: error rate must be below 1%, p99 latency must be below 500ms. Statistical tests catch subtle regressions: the Mann-Whitney U test detects distribution shifts (the canary's latency distribution is shifted higher than stable's, even if the mean is similar), the t-test detects mean changes, and a "Mann-Whitney U + effect size" combination distinguishes statistically significant regressions from noise. The analysis produces a score (0–100); above the threshold (typically 95), promote; below, roll back. The trade-off is that automated analysis requires high-quality metrics (RED metrics — rate, errors, duration — at minimum, plus business KPIs) and a baseline of historical variance to know what "noise" looks like; for new services with sparse metrics, the analysis is unreliable and human judgment is still needed.

The fourth concept is automated rollback. The value of a canary is not in detecting the regression but in responding to it — rolling traffic back to the stable version before the regression spreads. A mature canary system automates this: if canary analysis fails at any stage, the orchestrator shifts traffic back to 100% stable within seconds (a single router update), terminates the canary, and alerts the team. This is the "fail-safe" property: the worst case is a few minutes of degraded service for 1% of users, not a multi-hour outage for 100%. Netflix's Spinnaker, Argo Rollouts, and Flagger all support automated rollback with configurable conditions (metric thresholds, statistical confidence, manual override). The discipline is to rehearse rollbacks: a canary system that has never rolled back in production will fail the first time it tries, because the rollback path is untested. Teams practicing canary deployment run "rollback drills" — deliberately triggering a rollback by deploying a broken version — to verify the rollback path works. Google's disaster recovery testing, Netflix's Chaos Monkey, and Amazon's GameDay exercises all include rollback rehearsal.

The fifth concept is the real-world implementations. Netflix's red/black canary on Spinnaker is the canonical example: every deployment runs through Kayenta-based canary analysis, and the platform handles hundreds of releases per day with a failure rate below 1%. Google's progressive deployment framework standardizes the staged rollout across their internal services — a new version of Search or Ads starts at 0.1% of traffic, with automated metric gates at each stage, and the entire progression from 0.1% to 100% typically takes 4–24 hours. Facebook's staged rollout (called "Quick Promo") starts with employees, then a small percentage of users, then a growing percentage over days, with each stage gated by both automated metrics and human review of user-reported issues. Microsoft's Safe Deployment System applies the same pattern to Windows and Office updates: a new build goes to the "Canary" ring (a few thousand users), then "Dev" (hundreds of thousands), then "Beta" (millions), then "Stable" (everyone), with telemetry gates between each ring. The pattern is universal — the differences are in the metrics, the stages, and the level of automation.

The sixth concept is the trade-off versus blue-green and rolling. Blue-green provides instant cutover and instant rollback but exposes all users at once — a subtle regression hits everyone before it is noticed. Canary provides gradual exposure that catches subtle regressions but is slower (the staged progression takes 30 minutes to hours) and more complex (the orchestrator, metric pipeline, and automated analysis are nontrivial to build). Rolling deployment is cheap and simple but has no instant rollback — you must redeploy the old version, which takes as long as the original rollout. In practice, mature teams combine the strategies: blue-green provides the two environments and the instant-rollback router, canary analysis provides the staged exposure within the blue-green flow, and rolling is reserved for routine stateless releases where the complexity of canary is not justified. The choice is not canary versus blue-green — it is canary within blue-green, with the router shifting 1% → 5% → 25% → 100% and rolling back to the warm stable environment if any stage fails. The trade-off summary: canary delivers the safest release at the cost of slower progression, metric-pipeline investment, and orchestrator complexity. For services with high traffic, frequent releases, or high cost of failure, canary is the default; for low-traffic or low-risk services, simpler strategies may suffice.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Canary deployment orchestrator with metric-based progressive rollout.
- Snapshot of a version's key metrics for canary analysis.
- Progressive canary rollout with auto-rollback.
- Simulate soaking for soak_seconds, then snapshot metrics.
- In production this is a Prometheus query over the soak window.
- Error rate: canary must be no worse than stable + small slack.
- Latency: canary p99 must be within +X% of stable.
- CPU: canary must not be wildly more CPU-bound.

**Defines:** `Metrics`, `Version`, `CanaryThresholds`, `CanaryOrchestrator`

```python
"""
Canary deployment orchestrator with metric-based progressive rollout.

Demonstrates the logic that production canary systems (Spinnaker/Kayenta,
Argo Rollouts, Flagger) perform: shift traffic in stages, collect metrics
at each stage, run statistical comparison, auto-rollback on regression.

Models the state machine and the analysis — does not call real cloud APIs.
"""
import time
import random
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Optional

@dataclass
class Metrics:
    """Snapshot of a version's key metrics for canary analysis."""
    error_rate: float        # 0.0 - 1.0
    p99_latency_ms: float
    cpu_pct: float
    rps: float               # requests per second (sample rate)
    samples: int = 0         # how many requests observed

@dataclass
class Version:
    name: str
    version: str
    metrics: Metrics = field(default_factory=lambda: Metrics(0, 0, 0, 0))

@dataclass
class CanaryThresholds:
    max_error_rate: float = 0.01              # hard: < 1%
    max_p99_latency_ms: float = 500.0         # hard: < 500ms
    max_latency_regression_pct: float = 20.0  # relative: within +20% of stable
    min_score: float = 95.0                   # statistical: score >= 95 to promote
    min_samples: int = 1000                   # need enough data for stats

class CanaryOrchestrator:
    """Progressive canary rollout with auto-rollback."""

    # Stages: (traffic_pct_to_canary, soak_seconds)
    STAGES = [(1, 300), (5, 600), (25, 900), (100, 0)]

    def __init__(self, stable: Version, canary: Version,
                 thresholds: CanaryThresholds = CanaryThresholds()):
        self.stable = stable
        self.canary = canary
        self.thresholds = thresholds
        self.traffic_pct_canary = 0
        self.history: List[Dict] = []
        self.rolled_back = False

    def _log(self, stage: str, msg: str) -> None:
        self.history.append({"stage": stage, "msg": msg,
                             "canary_pct": self.traffic_pct_canary,
                             "ts": time.time()})
        print(f"  [{stage:>8}] canary={self.traffic_pct_canary:>3}%  {msg}")

    def _shift(self, pct: int) -> None:
        self.traffic_pct_canary = pct
        if pct == 0:
            self._log("rollback", "0% canary, 100% stable (auto-rollback)")
        elif pct == 100:
            self._log("cutover", "100% canary, stable drained")
        else:
            self._log("shift", f"{pct}% canary, {100-pct}% stable")

    def _collect_metrics(self, probe: Callable[[Version], Metrics],
                         soak_seconds: int) -> None:
        """Simulate soaking for soak_seconds, then snapshot metrics."""
        self._log("soak", f"collecting metrics for {soak_seconds}s "
                          f"({self.canary.version} canary vs "
                          f"{self.stable.version} stable)")
        # In production this is a Prometheus query over the soak window.
        self.canary.metrics = probe(self.canary)
        self.stable.metrics = probe(self.stable)

    def _statistical_score(self) -> float:
        """
        Compute a canary score 0-100.

        Real systems (Kayenta) use Mann-Whitney U for distribution shifts and
        t-tests for mean changes. Here we use a simplified relative-regression
        score combining error rate, latency, and CPU.
        """
        s, c = self.stable.metrics, self.canary.metrics
        if c.samples < self.thresholds.min_samples:
            self._log("stats", f"insufficient samples ({c.samples}), "
                               f"cannot analyze")
            return 0.0
        scores = []
        # Error rate: canary must be no worse than stable + small slack.
        err_slack = max(s.error_rate * 1.1, 0.001)
        scores.append(100.0 if c.error_rate <= s.error_rate + err_slack
                      else max(0, 100 - (c.error_rate - s.error_rate) * 1000))
        # Latency: canary p99 must be within +X% of stable.
        if s.p99_latency_ms > 0:
            reg = ((c.p99_latency_ms - s.p99_latency_ms)
                   / s.p99_latency_ms * 100)
            if reg > self.thresholds.max_latency_regression_pct:
                scores.append(max(0, 100 - reg * 2))
            else:
                scores.append(100.0)
        else:
            scores.append(100.0)
        # CPU: canary must not be wildly more CPU-bound.
        if s.cpu_pct > 0:
            cpu_reg = ((c.cpu_pct - s.cpu_pct) / s.cpu_pct * 100)
            scores.append(max(0, 100 - cpu_reg * 2))
        else:
            scores.append(100.0)
        return sum(scores) / len(scores)

    def analyze(self) -> bool:
        """Decide whether the canary is healthy enough to advance."""
        c = self.canary.metrics
        # Hard thresholds first.
        if c.error_rate > self.thresholds.max_error_rate:
            self._log("analyze", f"FAIL error_rate {c.error_rate:.3f} > "
                                 f"{self.thresholds.max_error_rate}")
            return False
        if c.p99_latency_ms > self.thresholds.max_p99_latency_ms:
            self._log("analyze", f"FAIL p99 {c.p99_latency_ms:.0f}ms > "
                                 f"{self.thresholds.max_p99_latency_ms:.0f}ms")
            return False
        # Statistical score.
        score = self._statistical_score()
        if score < self.thresholds.min_score:
            self._log("analyze", f"FAIL score {score:.1f} < "
                                 f"{self.thresholds.min_score}")
            return False
        self._log("analyze", f"PASS score {score:.1f} "
                             f"(canary err={c.error_rate:.3f} "
                             f"p99={c.p99_latency_ms:.0f}ms)")
        return True

    def rollback(self) -> None:
        self._shift(0)
        self.rolled_back = True

    def deploy(self, probe: Callable[[Version], Metrics],
               smoke: Optional[Callable[[Version], bool]] = None) -> bool:
        print(f"== canary deploy {self.canary.version} "
              f"(stable={self.stable.version}) ==")
        if smoke and not smoke(self.canary):
            self._log("smoke", "FAIL smoke tests, abort")
            return False
        self._log("smoke", "PASS smoke tests")
        for pct, soak in self.STAGES:
            self._shift(pct)
            self._collect_metrics(probe, soak)
            if not self.analyze():
                self.rollback()
                print("== canary FAILED, rolled back to stable ==")
                return False
        print("== canary SUCCEEDED, canary is new stable ==")
        return True

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Stable v1.5 has healthy production metrics.
    stable = Version("stable", "v1.5")
    # Canary v1.6 is the new release; metrics returned by probe below.
    canary = Version("canary", "v1.6")

    # Probe simulates Prometheus query: returns metrics for the version.
    def probe(v: Version) -> Metrics:
        if v.version == "v1.5":
            return Metrics(error_rate=0.005, p99_latency_ms=200,
                           cpu_pct=45, rps=990, samples=10000)
        # v1.6 canary: healthy in this run.
        return Metrics(error_rate=0.004, p99_latency_ms=210,
                       cpu_pct=47, rps=10, samples=10000)

    def smoke(v: Version) -> bool:
        return v.version == "v1.6"  # would call /health, /smoke

    orch = CanaryOrchestrator(stable, canary)
    ok = orch.deploy(probe, smoke)

    print("\n== history ==")
    for h in orch.history:
        print(f"  {h['stage']:>8}  canary={h['canary_pct']:>3}%  {h['msg']}")
    print(f"\nresult: {'SUCCESS' if ok else 'ROLLED BACK'}")
    print(f"stable={stable.version} canary={canary.version} "
          f"traffic_on_canary={orch.traffic_pct_canary}%")
```
